第一步是构造连续 CoT 目标。作者假设训练数据里有显式文本 CoT d1:L 和最终答案 x1:N。先用一个 encoder 把文本 CoT 压缩成长度为 K、维度为 D 的连续表示 e1:K。这里的 e-space 更像“压缩后的思维表示”，适合承载语义，但未必适合直接做 prompt-conditioned AR 生成。

第二步是引入一个更适合自回归建模的 LLM-facing thought space u1:K。作者不直接对 e 建模，而是通过可逆变换 Fθ 把 e 映射到 u。u-space 服从因果高斯分布：每个 thought token ui 的均值和方差由 prompt 以及前面的 thought tokens 因果决定。这样一来，u 可以像文本 token 一样左到右采样，并且整条 thought sequence 的 likelihood 可精确计算。e 和 u 之间用 normalizing flow 连接，利用变量替换公式把连续 thought 的精确密度写出来。这里的关键不是“用了 flow”这么简单，而是 flow 被用来桥接“语义压缩空间”和“易于 AR 生成的空间”。这比直接在 encoder latent 上做 diffusion 更贴近语言模型接口。

第三步是在同一个 LLM backbone 上联合建模 thought 和 answer。模型有共享的 causal backbone，上面接两个 head：一个是 continuous thought 的 NF / Gaussian density head，另一个是文本答案的 LM head。训练目标是联合最大化 latent thought 与最终答案的 likelihood。由于 thought likelihood 是 tractable 的，作者还能进一步在连续 thought 空间上做 policy-gradient 优化，而不是只能在离散文本 CoT 上做 RL。这一点把 supervised latent CoT 和 RL refinement 接到了同一概率接口上。

从与现有方法的区别看：相对 Coconut，这里是随机的、可评分的 latent path，而不是确定性 hidden rollout；相对 diffusion latent reasoning，这里是单次左到右采样，不需要多步去噪；相对先学 VAE 再单独训 latent generator 的两阶段方案，这里更强调与主干 LLM 的统一因果建模和答案生成耦合。4e:T817,The method has three main components.

First, the model defines a continuous target for chain-of-thought. Given supervised examples with prompt q, explicit textual CoT d1:L, and answer x1:N, an encoder compresses the textual rationale into a continuous sequence e1:K of length K and dimension D. This e-space is optimized for semantic compression, but it is not necessarily easy to model autoregressively conditioned on the prompt.

Second, the paper introduces an LLM-facing thought space u1:K that is easier to sample and score causally. Instead of modeling e directly, NF-CoT maps e to u through an invertible transformation Fθ. In the u-space, the thought sequence follows a causal Gaussian density: each latent thought token is generated left-to-right with mean and variance conditioned on the prompt and previous thought tokens. Because the transformation is invertible, the exact density of the original continuous thought can be computed via the change-of-variables formula. This is the key design choice. The flow is not used merely as a generic density estimator; it bridges a semantically meaningful compressed space and an autoregressively tractable space.

Third, the model jointly generates latent thoughts and textual answers using a shared causal LLM backbone. On top of the backbone, one head models the continuous thought density and another head models the answer tokens. Training maximizes the joint likelihood of latent thoughts and answers. Since the thought likelihood is tractable, the same interface also supports policy-gradient optimization directly in the continuous reasoning space.

Relative to prior work, the distinctions are sharp. Compared with Coconut-style methods, NF-CoT is stochastic and likelihood-based rather than deterministic hidden-state rollout. Compared with diffusion-based latent reasoning, it supports one-pass left-to-right sampling instead of iterative denoising. Compared with two-stage VAE-plus-generator pipelines, it more tightly couples latent-thought generation with the causal LM backbone and answer generation.4f:T65d,The evaluation is conducted on code reasoning and program synthesis benchmarks: MBPP, MBPP+, HumanEval, HumanEval+, and LiveCodeBench v6. NF-CoT is compared against explicit textual CoT and prior latent-reasoning baselines. The headline result is that NF-CoT improves pass rates while reducing intermediate reasoning cost, because the latent thought sequence K is much shorter than the token length of textual CoT.

The more informative results are in the analyses. One set of ablations studies the effect of latent thought length, showing a real trade-off between compression and generative ease rather than a monotonic benefit from longer latent traces. Another set examines likelihood-based sampling and reranking: because the latent reasoning path has an explicit probability model, the system can sample and score reasoning trajectories in a way that many latent-CoT methods cannot. The policy-gradient refinement experiments further show that the tractable density is operationally useful, not just mathematically elegant: continuous thought trajectories can be optimized with RL and yield additional gains.

The exact numbers matter less than the closed loop the paper demonstrates: explicit CoT supervision is compressed into continuous thoughts; those thoughts are modeled with exact likelihood; inference remains causal and one-pass; and the same latent space can be refined with policy gradients. When reading the experiments, pay special attention to token-cost comparisons against explicit CoT, sampling-efficiency comparisons against diffusion-style latent reasoning, and ablations on flow design and latent length.50:T594,Read it in the order of problem, interface, implementation, then experiments. Start with the introduction and preliminaries to understand the four properties the paper tries to preserve at once: autoregressive sampling, likelihood scoring, KV-cache compatibility, and joint generation of reasoning plus answer. Many latent-reasoning papers preserve only one or two of these.

In the method section, focus on the division of labor between the e-space and the u-space, and on why the flow is necessary. If only one idea is retained, it should be this: the encoder latent e is good for compressing rationale semantics, but the flow-transformed u is the space designed for causal generation and scoring by the LLM. Then inspect the joint objective to see how continuous-thought likelihood and answer-token likelihood are coupled.

In the experiments, prioritize the main result tables, latent-length ablations, sampling and reranking analysis, and the policy-gradient refinement section. Those are enough to build a solid understanding in roughly 45 minutes. For deeper reading, three questions are worth keeping in mind: whether the latent thoughts capture reusable reasoning structure or merely a compact rationale code; whether invertibility and tractable likelihood remain efficient at larger scales; and whether this latent causal stream could be introduced during pretraining rather than only through explicit CoT supervision.51:T7b9,技术路线是把 score field S 与一个 Schrödinger operator 建立对应。若 S=∇logρ，则定义 Score Hamiltonian 为 H^ = -∇² + Q_-(ρ)，其中 Q_- = (∇²√ρ)/√ρ；在 ρ 严格为正时，也可仅用 score 写成 -∇² + 1/2 ∇·S + 1/4 ||S||²。这个构造的关键性质有三个。其一，√ρ 是该算子的基态，且本征值为 0。其二，把 Fokker-Planck 中的密度 μ_τ 做 ground-state transform，写成 Ψ_τ = μ_τ / √ρ_tτ 后，原来的扩散采样动力学变成一个带 gauge correction 的虚时间演化：∂_τ Ψ = -H_t Ψ - (ṫ/2) ∂_t logρ_t Ψ。其三，这样就能把“采样是否跟得上移动目标分布”转成“系统是否能绝热跟踪瞬时基态”。

在此基础上，作者证明了一个针对 time-inhomogeneous Fokker-Planck 的定量绝热定理。误差用 χ² divergence 或 total variation 控制，上界由两部分组成：初始条件记忆项，按有效谱隙指数衰减；以及有限速率造成的 lag 项，正比于 schedule 速度 |ṫ| 和 ||∂_t logρ_t||，并被有效谱隙 Γ 抑制。这里 Γ 不是裸谱隙 Δ，而是扣除了时间变化项后的 effective gap。

随后作者把这个框架用于 learned score 不精确的 diffusion model。定义在真实分布 ρ_t 和模型分布 ρ_t^θ 下的 L2 score error，推导终态误差上界，并给出匹配下界。核心结论是：score error 的影响受谱隙调制，终态存在约 ε_score / √Δ 的误差地板。也就是说，分布几何越差、混合越慢、Poincaré 常数越大，训练误差越难在采样时被“洗掉”。

从方法区别看，已有 diffusion 理论常从 SDE 离散化误差、概率流 ODE、或 log-Sobolev / mixing 分析切入；这篇文章的特点是把 learned score 直接编码进一个可谱分析的 Hamiltonian，并把采样解释成 ground-state tracking。这种表述更适合讨论谱结构、激发态、以及 schedule 设计。52:T85e,The core construction maps a score field to a Schrödinger operator. For a conservative score S = grad log rho, the Score Hamiltonian is defined as H-hat = -Delta + Q_minus(rho), where Q_minus = (Delta sqrt rho) / sqrt rho. When rho is strictly positive, this can be written directly in terms of the score as -Delta + one-half div S + one-quarter norm(S)^2. This operator has three key properties. First, sqrt rho is its ground state with eigenvalue zero. Second, after the ground-state transform Psi_tau = mu_tau / sqrt(rho_ttau), the time-inhomogeneous Fokker-Planck equation becomes a simple imaginary-time evolution with a gauge term: partial_tau Psi = -H_t Psi - (dot t / 2) partial_t log rho_t Psi. Third, this turns diffusion sampling into a ground-state tracking problem.

Using that representation, the paper proves a quantitative adiabatic theorem for time-varying Fokker-Planck dynamics. The tracking error, measured in chi-squared divergence or total variation, has two components: a memory term from the initial condition that decays exponentially with an effective spectral gap, and a finite-rate lag term controlled by the schedule speed and the L2 norm of partial_t log rho_t, again suppressed by the effective gap. The effective gap is not just the raw spectral gap Delta; it is reduced by time-variation terms.

The framework is then extended to imperfectly learned scores. The authors define score errors under both the true interpolation density and the model density, and derive upper and matching lower bounds on the final discrepancy between the sampler and the target law. The main message is that score error is amplified according to the spectral geometry, yielding a terminal floor on the order of epsilon_score / sqrt(Delta). So poor mixing or narrow spectral gaps make training error harder to wash out at sampling time.

Compared with prior diffusion analyses based on discretization error, probability-flow ODEs, or generic mixing inequalities, the distinctive move here is to encode the learned score directly into a spectrally analyzable Hamiltonian and interpret sampling as adiabatic ground-state transport.53:T40f,The empirical section is mainly there to illustrate and validate the theory, not to benchmark generative quality at scale. A visually distinctive example uses a diffusion model trained on samples from the Hydrogen 1s orbital. From the learned score, the authors build the Score Hamiltonian and recover a spectrum that aligns with the known Hydrogen energy levels, including orbital structure shown in the figures. The point is not image quality or likelihood, but that the Hamiltonian spectrum captures meaningful geometric structure of the learned distribution.

More important are the numerical checks of the theory: figures such as 4 and 9 examine how tracking error depends on annealing speed, score error, and spectral gap, and whether the observed behavior follows the adiabatic bounds and the predicted error floor under imperfect scores. The excerpt does not include full tables, but the theory itself is stronger than a one-sided upper bound because the paper also provides matching lower bounds in the relevant local-rate regime.54:T450,Read this paper with a specific goal. Start from Section II and focus on equations (3) and (4): they define the Score Hamiltonian and show why the ground-state transform is the right change of variables. Then read Theorem II.1 carefully. The important part is the structure of the bound: one term for forgetting initialization, one term for finite-rate lag. After that, move to Theorem II.2 to see how learned score error enters the final sampling error, especially the epsilon_score over sqrt gap dependence. Only then go into the appendices for the technical assumptions on self-adjointness, form bounds, spectral gaps, and the lower-bound construction.

For a quick skim, 30 to 40 minutes on Section II plus Figures 2, 4, and 9 is enough. If you care about diffusion language models, the useful follow-up questions are: whether an analogous gap-controlled notion of sampling difficulty exists in discrete token spaces, whether schedule design can be informed by an effective-gap view, and whether the appendix treatment of non-conservative score fields can transfer to discrete or hybrid state spaces.55:T553,StateKV treats streaming prefill as approximating full self-attention using a small, fixed-size set of historical tokens.

Assumptions/observations:
- Most attention is intra-frame; inter-frame attention mass is concentrated on a small subset of historical tokens (“temporal sinks”) that evolve slowly.
- Therefore, cross-frame context can be carried by a constant-size memory K, independent of video length.

Mechanism:
- Maintain two coupled caches per layer:
  1) A fixed-capacity temporal state (size K) used for cross-frame attention. It is updated online by selecting historically important tokens (including sinks) based on an importance measure derived from attention weights.
  2) A per-frame cache that preserves full token detail for each frame, retained for the final text decoding stage.

Complexity profile:
- Prefill becomes O(N): each new frame attends cross-frame only to the fixed state plus its own intra-frame tokens.
- Decoding can still condition on all frame tokens (potentially O(N) in generation), but the paper argues prefill dominates in long-video QA, so linearizing prefill yields linear end-to-end scaling in practice.

Difference vs sliding-window streaming:
- Sliding windows impose a recency prior (hard truncation).
- StateKV uses importance-based retention to better match the full-attention behavior of the frozen backbone.56:T7ed,方法上这是一个控制变量做得比较严的测量研究。作者选了三类 7–8B GQA Transformer：Qwen-2.5-7B、Mistral-7B-v0.3、Llama-3.1-8B；四张 NVIDIA GPU：H100 SXM5、A100-80GB SXM4、L40S、L4；上下文长度覆盖 2048 到 16384；统一 batch=1、bf16 权重、SDPA attention、固定软件栈与 warmup 流程。核心分析指标是 observed-over-floor ratio，定义为实测 step time 与理论下界 t_floor=(W+K)/B_peak 的比值。这里 W 是每步需要流过显存的权重，K 是活跃 KV cache，B_peak 是峰值 HBM 带宽。若 decode 真被 HBM 带宽主导，这个比值应接近常数，且快卡应更接近理论下界。实测却发现，随着 GPU 峰值带宽升高，达到峰值带宽的比例反而下降，说明瓶颈从“搬不动数据”转向了“发不动 kernel”。

作者没有停在相关性判断，而是做了一个针对机制的可证伪 A/B：用 CUDA Graphs 只消除 launch overhead，不改动算子本身，比较 eager 与 graphed 的单 session 延迟。如果 H100 的短上下文瓶颈真是 launch tax，那么图捕获应带来明显收益；如果不是，则收益应很小。结果支持前者，并且在 L4 上得到近似空结果，形成了比较干净的机制区分。

另一个技术点是 attention backend 的 backend-pinned 对比。作者在 H100 的 batch-1 single-decode 形状下，固定后端分别测 PyTorch 默认 SDPA dispatcher、显式 FlashAttention context、FlashInfer、FlashAttention-3，发现默认 SDPA 反而最好。这说明在这个 shape 上，研究者常以为更快的专用 attention kernel 并不是主矛盾。相对地，在 L4 上，量化路径和 kernel 实现差异更关键。作者比较了 bf16、bnb-nf4、AutoAWQ+Marlin、GPTQ+ExLlamaV2，发现 Ada SM89 上 ExLlamaV2 的实现优势远大于“是否量化”这个抽象标签本身。也就是说，决定 batch-1 decode 延迟的不是单一因素，而是硬件代际、launch 开销、kernel 调度、量化实现四者的组合。57:T80f,实验覆盖 44 个有效测量单元，另有 4 个 L4 长上下文 OOM 被作者诊断为 A/B 协议伪影而非真实容量上限。最关键的结果有几组。

第一组是理论带宽下界与实测的偏离。作者报告 observed-over-floor ratio 在 L4 短上下文上约为 0.8，在 H100 短上下文上约为 0.25。换成 achieved bandwidth 的说法，L4 大约能打到峰值 HBM 带宽的 81%，H100 只有 27%。这意味着如果按“纯带宽受限”去估算 H100 相对 L4 的收益，会高估约 3 倍左右。这个结论直接否定了“更高 HBM 带宽就按比例降低 batch-1 decode latency”的简单部署逻辑。

第二组是 CUDA Graphs 的机制验证。在 H100、ctx=2048、N=10 个独立 Modal session 的 headline cell 上，within-session graphed/eager speedup 为 1.259x，95% bootstrap CI 为 [1.253, 1.267]，cross-session CV 仅 0.9%。同样条件下，L4 只有 1.028x。作者还给出了可证伪阈值：如果 H100 大多数 session 的收益低于约 1.15x，或 L4 任一 session 超过约 1.15x，则“launch-tax 主导 H100 短上下文 decode”这个解释就站不住。实测没有出现这种情况。

第三组是 H100 上 attention backend 的排序。在 batch-1 single-decode 形状下，PyTorch 默认 SDPA dispatcher 的 per-layer 时间为 36.05us，优于显式 FLASH_ATTENTION context 的 44.35us、FlashInfer 的 48.20us，以及 FlashAttention-3 的 79.25us。这个结果很反直觉，但很重要：在这种形状上，切换到更“激进”的 attention backend 不一定更快，甚至可能更慢。

第四组是 L4 上量化与 kernel 路径的对比。Qwen-2.5-7B 在 L4 上，bf16 为 62.32ms/step，AutoAWQ+Marlin 为 45.24ms/step，而 GPTQ+ExLlamaV2 可降到 17.36ms/step，较 bf16 提升 3.59x。作者进一步把它与 H100+CUDA Graphs 的 11.78ms/step 对比，指出对 physical AI 这类流式 workload，便宜卡上选对 kernel，缩小的差距比单纯升级到更贵 GPU 还要大。这也是文中“cost-per-token ladder inversion”的核心证据。58:T44b,This is not a pretraining-method paper, but it is highly relevant to foundation-model deployment and to system choices that feed back into model design. Its contribution is a careful correction to a widely repeated systems assumption. First, it shows that for batch-1 decode, faster silicon does not automatically translate into proportional latency gains, even when peak HBM bandwidth is much higher. That affects cost-per-token estimates and can influence decisions around model size, context length, GQA design, and quantization strategy. Second, it offers a practical diagnostic split: on H100-like hardware, investigate launch overhead first; on L4-like hardware, investigate kernel implementation and quantized execution paths first. Third, it is targeted at physical-AI workloads rather than cloud serving, which is important because many serving intuitions are inherited from high-throughput settings and do not transfer cleanly to low-batch, latency-critical inference. The contribution is empirical rather than algorithmic, but the result is strong enough to change engineering priorities.59:T920,The paper is a controlled measurement study. It evaluates three 7–8B GQA transformers—Qwen-2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Llama-3.1-8B—across four NVIDIA GPUs: H100 SXM5, A100-80GB SXM4, L40S, and L4. Context lengths range from 2048 to 16384. The setup is fixed to batch size 1, bf16 weights, SDPA attention, controlled warmup, and a consistent software stack on Modal hosts.

The central metric is the observed-over-floor ratio, R_floor = t_obs / t_floor, where t_floor = (W + K) / B_peak. Here W is the weight traffic per decode step, K is the active KV-cache traffic, and B_peak is peak HBM bandwidth. If batch-1 decode were truly dominated by HBM bandwidth, this ratio should remain relatively stable and fast GPUs should approach the floor more closely. Instead, the ratio drops as peak bandwidth increases, which implies that the bottleneck shifts away from raw memory transfer and toward launch-side overhead.

The key methodological strength is that the paper does not stop at correlation. It runs a falsifiable A/B test with CUDA Graphs, chosen specifically because graph capture reduces launch overhead while leaving the underlying kernels largely unchanged. If H100 short-context decode is launch-bound, graphing should produce a clear speedup; if not, the gain should be small. The result supports the launch-tax interpretation on H100 and gives a near-null result on L4, which is exactly the contrast the mechanism predicts.

A second technical contribution is the backend-pinned attention comparison on H100 at the exact batch-1 single-decode shape. The paper compares PyTorch’s default SDPA dispatcher against explicit FlashAttention context, FlashInfer, and FlashAttention-3, and finds that default SDPA is fastest in this regime. That is useful because it shows that attention-kernel choice is not the main constraint on H100 for this workload. By contrast, on L4 the decisive factor is the quantized execution path and kernel implementation. The comparison among bf16, bnb-nf4, AutoAWQ+Marlin, and GPTQ+ExLlamaV2 shows that implementation details dominate the practical latency outcome on Ada SM89. The broader message is that batch-1 decode latency is shaped by an interaction among hardware generation, launch overhead, backend choice, and quantization kernel quality, not by a single “memory-bound” label.5a:T8e6,The study reports 44 valid measurement cells, with 4 additional L4 long-context OOM cases diagnosed as A/B protocol artifacts rather than true capacity limits. Several results carry most of the paper.

First, the gap between the HBM-bandwidth floor and actual latency widens on faster GPUs. The observed-over-floor ratio is about 0.8 on L4 at short context and about 0.25 on H100 at short context. In achieved-bandwidth terms, L4 reaches roughly 81% of peak HBM bandwidth on this workload, while H100 reaches only 27%. That means the simple HBM-bound model overpredicts the speedup from moving to H100 by roughly a factor of three for this workload class.

Second, the CUDA Graphs falsification test strongly supports the launch-overhead explanation. On the H100 headline cell at context length 2048 with N=10 independent Modal sessions, the within-session graphed versus eager speedup is 1.259x, with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of [1.253, 1.267], and cross-session coefficient of variation of only 0.9%. On L4 at the same cell, the gain is only 1.028x. The paper also states explicit falsification thresholds: the launch-tax interpretation would have been undermined if H100 gains were mostly below about 1.15x, or if L4 showed gains above about 1.15x. Neither happened.

Third, the backend-pinned attention comparison on H100 is striking. At the batch-1 single-decode shape, PyTorch’s default SDPA dispatcher runs at 36.05 microseconds per layer, faster than explicit FlashAttention context at 44.35 microseconds, FlashInfer at 48.20 microseconds, and FlashAttention-3 at 79.25 microseconds. So in this regime, swapping to a more specialized attention backend does not solve the main problem and can even hurt.

Fourth, the L4 quantization comparison shows that kernel path matters more than the abstract quantization label. For Qwen-2.5-7B on L4, bf16 takes 62.32 ms per step, AutoAWQ+Marlin reduces this to 45.24 ms, and GPTQ+ExLlamaV2 reaches 17.36 ms, a 3.59x speedup over bf16. The paper then compares this with H100 plus CUDA Graphs at 11.78 ms per step. The practical implication is that for streaming physical-AI workloads, choosing the right kernel path on cheaper hardware can close more of the latency gap than simply moving to a much more expensive GPU.5b:T6da,This is a skim-level paper, but it rewards a focused read. The right way to read it is to keep one question in mind: are you trying to understand why H100 underdelivers relative to bandwidth expectations, or are you trying to make a deployment decision across L4, L40S, A100, and H100?

If you have 20–30 minutes, prioritize four parts. First, read the introduction carefully for workload definition. The paper is about single-stream, batch-1, autoregressive decode, not high-throughput cloud serving. The conclusions are shape-specific.

Second, read the section that defines the floor model and the observed-over-floor ratio. This is the conceptual anchor of the paper. The authors are not building a complicated performance model; they are using a simple lower bound to test whether the standard HBM-bound story is sufficient.

Third, spend time on the CUDA Graphs A/B experiment. This is the most important section. Pay attention to what the intervention changes and what it intentionally does not change. The value of the paper comes from this mechanism-level test, not just from the raw latency table.

Fourth, inspect the backend-pinned attention matrix and the L4 quantization matrix directly. The former is useful if you are tempted to assume FlashAttention-3 must be best on H100. The latter is useful if you treat quantization as a single knob rather than a combination of quantization format and execution kernel.

A good follow-up question is how far the result generalizes: larger models, different layer counts, longer contexts, paged KV cache, and other runtimes such as vLLM or TensorRT-LLM. The paper is convincing for 7–8B GQA, bf16, SDPA, and single-stream decode, but broader deployment claims still need additional measurements.5c:T49e,The framework is trace-aware and has two components:
1) TSPD (Temporal-Spatial Parallel Decoding): a lightweight temporal-spatial controller predicts, per position, whether a token is ready to be fixed/committed. Inputs are short-horizon trajectory features over recent steps—confidence, entropy, and a momentum-like change statistic—augmented with relative position within a block to capture positional effects. A shared sequential perception model is used to recognize regimes that defeat step-local rules (steady growth, underconfident-but-correct, oscillatory confidence, delayed stabilization).
2) CE (Confidence Extrapolation): a training-free plug-in module that models confidence evolution with a simple state-space process, forecasting near-future confidence along with uncertainty. A risk-aware horizon rule limits look-ahead based on forecast uncertainty and left-context progress, so extrapolation is only applied when the recent trace supports it.
TSPD improves the correctness of commit decisions; CE reduces “waiting time” when trends are predictable. Both operate purely at decoding time and are designed to compose with system optimizations like KV caching.5d:T81e,方法核心有两部分。第一部分是把目标模型切成 n 个 pipeline stages。这样在任一 cycle 内，模型不是让一个 token 走完整个网络，而是让 n 个 token 分别位于不同深度并行推进。为了避免 bubble，每个 cycle 都需要有一个新 token 被送入第一阶段。SPD 的 speculation module 就负责预测这个 token。

第二部分是 speculation module 的设计。作者没有像 PPSD 那样只用第一阶段的浅层 hidden state 做 early exit，而是做 multi-depth feature aggregation：收集当前流水线中各 token 在不同 stage 的部分特征，以及已经验证 token 的完整特征，再把这些信息聚合后预测下一个 token。这样做的关键原因是，预测时不再只依赖某个很浅的局部表示，而是利用了“多 token、多深度”的上下文切片。论文强调一个重要性质：由于流水线长度固定为 n，预测所依赖的不完整特征的缺失程度被上界在常数 n 内，不会像传统 multi-token drafting 那样随着 draft length 增长而无界恶化。

另一个关键设计是 zero mutual waiting。常规 speculative decoding 中，草稿往往要等 target model 产出某些状态后才能继续。SPD 把 speculation module 的执行窗口前移，只基于当前 cycle 的 pipeline 输入状态来预测下一 token，而不是等本 cycle 输出出来后再预测。这样 speculation 和 target pipeline step 可以严格并行。代价是预测时可用信息更早、更少，理论上更难；作者用更强的 multi-depth aggregation 来补偿，并指出因为该模块延迟被 target step 完全掩蔽，所以可以把 speculation network 做得更深而不增加端到端时延。

论文还提出了 Equivalent Acceptance Length 这一指标，用来替代传统 acceptance length。原因是 pipeline speculative decoding 里存在初始化和 flush penalty，简单统计接受 token 数会高估真实收益。这个指标把 rejection 后流水线清空、重新填充的代价算进去，更接近理论吞吐提升。5e:T830,SPD has two central components. First, the target LLM is partitioned into n pipeline stages. Instead of running one token through all layers, the model processes n tokens concurrently at different depths. To avoid bubbles, each cycle must inject one new token into stage 1. The speculation module predicts exactly that token.

Second, the speculation module uses multi-depth feature aggregation. Unlike PPSD, which only uses shallow hidden states from the first stage, SPD collects partially processed features from tokens currently inside the pipeline, together with fully processed features from already verified tokens. These features are aggregated to predict the next token. The key argument is that prediction is grounded in richer and better-aligned internal states from the target model itself, rather than in a shallow early-exit view. The paper emphasizes a bounded-difficulty property: because the pipeline length is fixed at n, the incompleteness of the available features is bounded by a constant, instead of growing unbounded with draft length as in conventional multi-token speculation.

A second key design is zero mutual waiting. SPD shifts the speculation window forward so that the speculation module runs from the current pipeline input state, not from the output state after the current pipeline step. This allows speculation and target execution to run strictly in parallel. The trade-off is that prediction is made from earlier, less complete information. The authors compensate with stronger multi-depth aggregation and argue that, since speculation latency is fully hidden behind the target pipeline step, the speculation network can be made deeper without increasing end-to-end latency.

The paper also introduces Equivalent Acceptance Length, a metric intended to better reflect pipelined speculative decoding. Standard acceptance length can overestimate gains because it ignores pipeline fill and flush costs after rejection. The new metric explicitly accounts for initialization overhead and rejection penalties, making the theoretical speedup analysis more faithful.5f:T58e,Experiments are conducted on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, evaluated on MT-Bench, GSM8K, and HumanEval. The main reported result is that SPD achieves comparable or better equivalent acceptance length and surpasses EAGLE-3 in theoretical speedup under most settings. The paper appears more careful about theoretical throughput than about claiming universal wall-clock dominance.

Around 30 to 45 minutes should be enough to extract the main idea and judge whether it is worth deeper follow-up.61:T6ce,The method, ART (Attention Run-time Termination), exploits a property of FlashAttention-style blockwise execution. Keys and values are processed block by block, and after each block the kernel already maintains an intermediate attention output O^(t). The paper observes that for many queries, O^(t) stabilizes well before all KV blocks are consumed.

Instead of predicting token importance ahead of time, ART monitors the evolution of these intermediate outputs during kernel execution. The termination rule is based on output stability in two senses:
1. scale stability: whether the norm of the incremental update has become sufficiently small over recent steps;
2. directional stability: whether the update direction is no longer meaningfully changing the output direction, indicating only minor same-direction corrections remain.

This matters because attention-score-based criteria are incomplete. A token can receive nontrivial attention weight but contribute little if its value vector is uninformative; conversely, a lower-weight token can still shift the output in an important direction through its value. By checking convergence directly in output space, ART implicitly captures the joint effect of keys and values.

Implementation-wise, ART is inserted into the blockwise attention kernel itself. It does not require a learned predictor, offline preprocessing, or extra passes over the cache. Since the relevant intermediate states already exist in the streaming softmax computation, the added cost is mainly lightweight bookkeeping and threshold checks. The paper also emphasizes orthogonality: ART can be layered on top of existing key-based KV management methods, acting as a runtime refinement after static candidate reduction.62:T51f,The evaluation focuses on long-context generation and LongBench-style settings, measuring throughput, latency, and quality retention. The headline result is that ART delivers more than 20% higher generation throughput at large batch sizes relative to strong baselines, with negligible quality loss. Importantly, ART is not framed as a full replacement for prior KV management methods; it is a runtime module that can be combined with them, so the gain comes from both fewer KV block fetches and less downstream attention computation.

The paper appears to include several useful analyses:
1. output-convergence visualizations showing that O^(t) often stabilizes early;
2. failure cases for key-only signals, illustrating why attention scores do not reliably track true output impact;
3. threshold ablations showing the trade-off between speed and quality;
4. compositional experiments where ART is added on top of existing KV pruning methods and still yields extra speedup.

The deeper questions are whether the stopping rule can be tied to an error bound, and whether the same output-convergence signal could inform adaptive sparse attention during training.64:T6b7,WaveFilter is a training-free KV-cache filtering framework built around multi-scale analysis with the discrete wavelet transform (DWT). The intuition is that not all cached tokens are equally useful in long contexts. A good system should first locate relevant regions cheaply, then refine the selection locally.

The method appears to operate in two stages. First, it performs coarse filtering. At the initial step, WaveFilter applies DWT to the cache representation to obtain a compressed multi-scale view of the sequence. The goal is to reduce cache length, suppress high-frequency noise, and preserve lower-frequency global structure. The current query then attends to this compressed representation to identify an initial set of important regions or tokens. Second, it performs fine filtering. Starting from those coarse candidates, the method uses multi-scale recursive filtering to progressively map back to finer temporal scales and identify the final critical tokens. These selected tokens are then used to construct a sparse KV cache dynamically for the current attention computation.

The main distinction from prior DLM cache methods is not a new cache update rule, but a front-end token selection mechanism that can sit on top of existing cache strategies. Methods such as Fast-dLLM and Elastic-Cache can accelerate short-text generation, but they struggle in long contexts because token retention becomes hard to tune. WaveFilter uses wavelet-based multi-scale structure to make that search cheaper: first global localization in a compressed domain, then recursive refinement in the original domain. The paper positions this as a universal plug-in, meaning it should work without changing model parameters.65:T588,From the available full-text content, the experiments are organized around two questions: whether WaveFilter preserves quality better on long-context tasks, and whether it improves throughput when combined with existing DLM cache methods. A draft source proposes a block of tokens; the target model verifies the block and commits the accepted prefix. The payoff variable is accepted length, the number of drafted tokens accepted at the current decoding state. The method combines two draft sources. The first is a parameter-free cache drafter, instantiated with a suffix cache similar to SuffixDecoding, which searches the prompt and generated history for suffix matches and reuses following spans. The second is a model-based drafter, such as the EAGLE family. Before verification, a lightweight predictor estimates the accepted length of the current cache draft. If the predicted payoff is high, the cache draft is verified. Otherwise, the system falls back to the model-based drafter. The predictor is trained by trace replay: generation traces are replayed to obtain accepted-length labels for cache drafts at different states. The target model and verification rule remain unchanged; the learned component only allocates verification across draft sources.68:T4b0,CaDDTree reframes draft-tree construction as throughput maximization.
- Setup: a block-diffusion drafter produces per-position marginals q_i in one forward pass (factorized joint Q), enabling tractable computation of node/prefix probabilities used by DDTree-style methods.
- Limitation of prior work: maximizing expected accepted length under Q (a surrogate for the target model) is non-decreasing in the node budget n=|T|, so it cannot determine the right budget; existing adaptive-shape methods still fix n offline.
- Key change: define a per-round throughput objective, roughly E[1+α(T)] / (draft_cost(n)+verify_cost(n)), where α is the number of accepted tokens and costs are explicit functions of tree size.
- Main theoretical lever: under a mild convexity assumption on verification cost (increasing marginal cost with n), throughput as a function of n becomes unimodal. This reduces budget selection to an efficient 1D search/greedy procedure that jointly grows the tree and decides when to stop, enabling per-round budget adaptation.
- Instantiation: the framework is implemented on top of block diffusion drafting plus tree-attention verification; no additional model training is required.69:T502,The framework has an offline placement pipeline plus a lightweight online guard, and intentionally leaves the router unchanged.
1) TACG (Task-Aware Coactivation Grouping):
- Split calibration traffic into task families (K=4 in the setup) and collect per-family expert usage and co-activation statistics per layer.
- Compute soft expert-to-family preferences, then reweight the co-activation graph into a task-modulated graph so that within-family co-activated experts become closer.
- Run spectral clustering on the modulated graph, followed by a capacity-repair step to satisfy per-GPU capacity constraints, producing a primary GPU assignment for each expert.
2) GESR (Generic Expert Shared Replication):
- Identify cross-family “generic” experts that tend to become hotspots using co-activation centrality and cross-family consistency.
- Replicate only this small set onto a few secondary GPUs chosen to be structurally compatible with the primary placement.
- At serving time, select among replicas using a locality- and load-aware rule with exponentially decayed load signals to mitigate skew under workload shift.
The design trades optimality for operational simplicity: no router changes, no dynamic migration; it relies on task-family partitioning and calibration traces.6a:T412,The method has two main components. Semantic Embedding Navigation builds the retrieval query from the target model hidden state under the current prefix, together with the current greedy anchor token. This projected query is used to retrieve candidate continuations from static datastores and dynamic contexts. The reason is straightforward: hidden states carry richer semantic intent than a discrete next-token key, so the candidate pool is less constrained by surface-form overlap. Soft-gated Evaluation then verifies prefix-plus-draft batches with the target model, but it does not enforce exact token matching everywhere. It uses entropy as a gate: low-entropy positions remain strict, while uncertain positions can be accepted through top-k distributional alignment. Using this lens, the authors project hidden states from consecutive layers through the final LM head with an early-exit strategy, obtaining per-layer token distributions. The difference between consecutive layer distributions is treated as a gradient-like update. They then compute the cosine similarity between adjacent gradient-like updates and call it driftance. A strongly negative driftance indicates that the later update sharply deviates from the previous direction, which the paper interprets as a sign that the current layer may be steering decoding toward hallucination. Once such a layer is detected, DeLask does not fully remove it. Instead, it applies partial skipping by aggregating the current layer output with the previous layer representation. The rationale is that hard skipping can break cross-layer coherence and damage useful computation, while partial skipping attenuates the harmful contribution without collapsing the residual pathway.6c:T53e,The evaluation spans three task groups—factual hallucination detection, multiple-choice reasoning, and open-ended generation—across seven benchmarks. From the task setup, though, the method appears more naturally aligned with factual QA and open-ended generation than with pure mathematical reasoning, because it targets factual drift rather than general reasoning competence.6d:T834,The key move is to replace weight-space reconstruction with output-space reconstruction after optimal low-rank correction. Let W be the pretrained weight matrix, W_hat its quantized version, X the calibration activations, and BA the LoRA-style low-rank correction. Instead of minimizing only ||W - W_hat||, the method minimizes a layerwise objective of the form ||(W - W_hat - BA)X||. This changes the problem in two important ways.

First, it becomes activation-aware. Errors are weighted by their actual effect on layer outputs under calibration inputs, rather than by raw weight discrepancy. This directly targets a weakness of weight-only approaches: some large weight errors barely matter functionally, while small errors along high-energy activation directions can be very damaging.

Second, the method explicitly separates correctable and uncorrectable quantization noise. The outer optimization over W_hat is encouraged to place dominant error components inside a low-rank subspace, while the inner optimization over BA captures the best local correction within that subspace. The authors describe this as structural noise shaping: not merely reducing error magnitude, but controlling its geometry.

Optimization is done by an alternating procedure. Intuitively, one step estimates the best low-rank corrective subspace for the current quantized layer, and the other performs quantization under a projection constraint so that the residual error is pushed toward that subspace. The orthogonal projection language is important: the goal is to minimize the residual component orthogonal to what the adapter can fix. The paper also claims theoretical guarantees on convergence and on preserving more downstream adaptation capacity than standard PTQ.

Relative to methods like LoftQ, the differences are clear: the objective is output-aware rather than weight-only, the method explicitly shapes the subspace structure of quantization noise rather than only co-initializing quantization and LoRA, and the paper emphasizes theoretical analysis rather than empirical initialization heuristics alone.6e:T592,From the provided full text, the main empirical claim is that ProjQ consistently outperforms standard PTQ+LoRA/QLoRA pipelines and LoftQ-like baselines across multiple benchmarks. A quick skim is 30–45 minutes; a careful read with theory and ablations is around 1–1.5 hours.70:T6f7,Fast-dLLM++ is a training-free replacement for the commit rule used during diffusion decoding. Instead of using only the weakest confidence among the top-n candidate positions, it keeps the full sorted confidence profile (c(1), c(2), ..., c(n)). For each candidate prefix of size n, it computes a Fréchet lower bound L_n on the probability that all n marginal greedy tokens are jointly correct, and an upper bound U_n on the probability of any competing tuple. The decoder commits the largest prefix satisfying L_n - U_n > delta, where delta is a safety margin.

The key technical move is that the certificate is built from marginal confidences only, with no explicit dependence model across positions. The paper proves that this yields a heterogeneous-confidence sufficient condition under which greedy parallel decoding matches the true joint greedy decision. It further argues that, without additional dependence information, the Fréchet-based certificate is the strongest conservative distribution-free guarantee available from marginals alone. This is the main theoretical claim.

Another useful result is the reduction to the previous rule: in the equal-confidence case, the new criterion collapses exactly to Fast-dLLM factor decoding. So the method is not a disconnected heuristic; it is a strict generalization of the homogeneous-confidence analysis. The heterogeneity-bonus decomposition then explains when gains appear: if the confidence profile has a strong head and a weaker tail, the full-profile certificate can still justify committing a larger set, whereas the weakest-token rule gets dominated by the tail. Operationally, the method remains compatible with KV caching and does not require a separate drafter or verifier, unlike speculative decoding for AR models.71:T494,The evaluation spans reasoning, math, code, and multimodal reasoning. Models include LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-v0-Base-7B, and LLaDA-V. Benchmarks include GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP. The main empirical claim is not a single-point accuracy gain but a better accuracy-throughput frontier: at matched quality, Fast-dLLM++ achieves higher throughput; at matched throughput, it preserves better accuracy than prior threshold/factor rules.

The theoretical discussion identifies why Frobenius-optimal tensor truncation can be misaligned with Transformer function preservation.73:T4cd,TreeFlash adds a lightweight AR-approximation layer to a DFlash-style one-shot drafter. For draft position t+i, the module takes the drafter hidden state and the embedding of the previous token, passes them through a SwiGLU MLP, and produces a modified hidden state. The verifier’s output embedding is then reused to produce q'(x_{t+i}|x_{≤t}, x_{t+i-1}). This gives a local autoregressive dependency without turning the drafter into a sequential model. To avoid sequentially applying the approximator across draft depth, the method uses a two-stage tree construction. First, it builds a top-M-ary tree using the original DFlash marginals. Stage one operates before visual tokens enter the LLM. Instead of ranking tokens only by attention, it formulates token selection with a potential-energy or repulsion-inspired objective: tokens are treated like charged particles in feature space, and semantically similar tokens repel each other more strongly. This encourages a selected subset that is spatially and semantically diverse, preserving global structure. Stage two operates inside an intermediate LLM layer and uses instruction-aware cross-attention to remove task-irrelevant visual tokens. The design is motivated by empirical analysis of representation dynamics. In deeper vision layers, feature-similar tokens receive increasingly similar attention scores, so attention loses discriminative power within local semantic neighborhoods. In the LLM decoder, earlier layers aggregate broad context while deeper layers become more task-focused. The paper also introduces a KNN Consistency Score to quantify how strongly feature similarity aligns with attention similarity, serving as a diagnostic for attention collapse. Compared with prior single-stage pruning methods, the novelty is not just adding another pruning step, but explicitly decoupling structural coverage from semantic relevance and using different signals for each stage.75:T42e,Experiments are conducted on multiple VLMs and benchmarks to evaluate the efficiency-performance trade-off. The most useful results to inspect are the performance curves across pruning ratios, the ablations for each stage, and the sensitivity to the layer where semantic pruning is inserted.76:T73e,AURA-Mem can be summarized as a frozen backbone plus a constant-size recurrent memory plus an action-driven write gate. There are four main ingredients. First, the model wraps a fixed-size memory around a frozen vision-language-action backbone, replacing the linearly growing KV cache with an O(1) state. Second, it introduces a learned action-utility write gate. The trigger is not perplexity, recency, or generic reconstruction error; it is whether the current observation would change the next action. If the new input is not useful for action selection, the memory does not write. Third, the training objective is an action-information bottleneck rather than observation reconstruction. The action-chunk loss is backpropagated through the gate decision so that the memory learns to retain what matters for acting well, not what best preserves token-level fidelity. Fourth, the method includes explicit write-rate control during training via a target write rate rho and a penalty weight gamma, allowing the model to move along an accuracy-versus-write-bandwidth frontier. The paper also instantiates the approximate information state framework empirically by measuring epsilon and delta for the learned memory and reporting an action-sufficiency certificate. The full value-loss bound remains loose because the Lipschitz-related term is too large at current scale, but the attempt is still notable: it turns 'is this compressed state sufficient for control?' into something measurable. Relative to SSM-style recurrent models, AURA-Mem does not write every step. Relative to KV-cache compression methods, it does not approximate a growing cache; it commits to constant memory from the start. Relative to Tensor Cache, it differs simultaneously in write trigger, training objective, write-rate conditioning, and the measured action-sufficiency analysis.77:T4c4,The main empirical claim is not superior task accuracy, but a better write-bandwidth frontier at matched performance. On memory-dependent synthetic benchmarks, AURA-Mem achieves 4.98x to 9.19x fewer memory writes than a write-everything dense baseline while maintaining statistical parity with the best O(1) baseline, fixed_size_state; the paired bootstrap confidence interval includes zero at N=64. The paper is careful about this framing: the result is reduced writes without collapsing task success, not universal accuracy dominance. On the theory-measurement side, the shipped checkpoint reports epsilon_mean = 0.0021 and epsilon_q95 = 0.0076. However, once the L_V term is included, the full bound is still vacuous, so the practically informative quantity is the measured epsilon rather than the final value-loss certificate. The experiments compare against several families: bounded-state models that write every step, KV-cache compression or eviction methods, and the structurally related Tensor Cache. If your interest is persistent inference on edge hardware or long-horizon agents, the results are meaningful. If your interest is pure LLM pretraining, the transfer path is less direct and needs interpretation.78:T439,The authors replace aggregate post-pruning accuracy with a capability-retention view over four dimensions: General, Commonsense, Code, and Math. They then profile 15 calibration sources using information metrics from Objective Information Theory. The strongest predictors are Distortion, operationalized through perplexity, and Aggregation, measured through repeated 4-gram patterns. Broader measures such as Scope, Variety, Granularity, and Mismatch are less reliable. Based on this analysis, the paper proposes two calibration constructions. The first is mix_balanced, which samples uniformly from capability-aligned pools under the same 128-sequence budget used by the baselines. 1) Adaptive retrieval (lexical-first, semantic fallback): use exact token matching on the most recent token as an anchor to retrieve prior positions in the unified memory (prompt + generated history). Only when lexical retrieval yields no candidates does it invoke semantic retrieval via representation similarity, expanding reachability while preserving the precision/latency profile of lexical matching. Candidates are then reranked by hidden-state similarity to pick an anchor most compatible with the current decoding state.
2) Adaptive reuse (draft tree instead of single span): starting from the selected anchor, it (a) copies a main continuation span when the anchor is lexically matched; (b) adds a small set of branch tokens sampled/selected from the target model’s next-token distribution to hedge ambiguity; (c) performs a successor reuse step to extend branches by one more reused token when alignment exists in memory. The resulting small draft tree is verified in one target-model pass using tree attention.
The key design constraint is cost control: semantic retrieval is conditional (no-hit only), and branching is kept small so verification overhead does not erase speed gains.7b:T7c0,The method, Efficient Operator Search (EOS), starts from a frozen multimodal foundation model and parameterizes three decisions that are usually hand-crafted: which layers perform reduction, how many tokens are retained at each layer, and which reduction behavior is used.

The first key piece is the unified operator family. At an active reduction layer, EOS selects K anchor tokens using an importance score and treats the remaining tokens as reduction candidates. It then computes normalized similarities between candidate tokens and anchors. A temperature parameter τ controls the sharpness of the assignment: low τ approaches hard nearest-anchor merging, while high τ produces softer redistribution or pooling-like behavior. A transfer gate determines whether information from discarded tokens is removed or preserved and transferred to anchors. With the gate off, the operator behaves like pruning; with the gate on, different τ regimes recover merging, pooling, or soft reweighting. The central claim is that these common operators are not isolated tricks but different regions of one shared continuous space.

The second piece is the search space. EOS does not only search operator regimes; it also searches layer activation and retention budgets. In other words, layer selection, token budgets, and operator parameters are all learnable. Discrete choices are relaxed into differentiable forms so that optimization can proceed through expected task loss under sampled policies and efficiency constraints.

The third piece is the objective. The search optimizes a trade-off between task loss and computational cost while keeping the backbone frozen. This makes the method cheaper than retraining and more aligned with deployment-time optimization. Relative to methods such as ToMe or SparseVLM, the novelty is not a new fixed compression rule, but a shared parameterization that contains several known rules as special cases and lets the search discover layer-wise hybrids.7c:T5f4,The experiments are designed to establish two points: first, the unified space can recover strong hand-designed baselines; second, searching over that space yields better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than using a single manually chosen operator. The paper evaluates EOS on representative multimodal benchmarks and compares against pruning- and merging-based baselines. The reported outcome is that EOS can reproduce known operating regimes while also finding better hybrid configurations under similar token or compute budgets.

The most informative part is the ablation structure rather than any single headline number. The paper separates the effects of searching layer positions, searching token budgets, searching operator regimes, and jointly searching all of them. Joint search performs best, which suggests strong coupling between where compression happens, how much compression is applied, and how information is transferred. Another important ablation studies τ and the transfer gate: τ controls the transition from hard merge to soft pooling-like behavior, while the gate controls whether reduced tokens are dropped or preserved through redistribution.

The provided full-text excerpt does not include the complete numerical tables, exact model sizes, or benchmark-by-benchmark gains, so it would be unsafe to invent precise numbers. What is clear from the paper’s structure and claims is that the benefit comes from shifting the overall trade-off frontier rather than from an isolated gain on one benchmark.7d:T4f5,For a quick read, start with the introduction and the main figures that illustrate the operator space. The key idea is that pruning, merging, pooling, and reweighting are different regimes of one parameterized family rather than unrelated methods. Then read the method section carefully, especially the roles of assignment temperature τ, the transfer gate, layer activation, and retention budget. That is where the paper’s real content sits.

A natural next step would be to ask what happens if the same continuous operator space is introduced during pretraining or continued pretraining.7e:T8eb,Tangram 的技术路线围绕一个关键观察展开：不同 attention head 需要保留多少历史 token，这种 retention pattern 在同一模型内是相对稳定、可预先估计的，而不是每个请求都剧烈变化。基于这个观察，作者把原本需要在线决定的异构 KV 管理，改写成一个尽量静态、可预编排的问题。

第一部分是 Deterministic Budget Allocation。传统非均匀压缩如果按请求动态回收 KV，会产生大量控制面开销，因为系统要跟踪每个 head、每个 page 的占用与释放。Tangram 直接为各 head 预分配确定性的 retention budget，把动态 reclaim 变成静态 footprint 规划。这样做的好处是把复杂的在线内存管理前移，减少 runtime bookkeeping。代价是灵活性下降，但作者的前提是 head-wise pattern 足够稳定，因此这个取舍成立。

第二部分是 Head Group Page。现有 paged KV 设计通常以统一 page 结构管理所有 heads，适合均匀长度，不适合异构长度，因为某些 head 压缩后释放不出完整 page，形成严重内部碎片。Tangram 将具有相近 budget 的 heads 分组，给每组建立独立 page table。这样 page 的物理回收粒度更贴近真实保留长度，能显著减少 fragmentation。为了避免 page table 操作本身成为 CPU 瓶颈，作者还实现了 vectorized block table，用 CPU SIMD 并行处理映射与查表。

第三部分是 Ahead-of-Time Load Balancing。非均匀 KV 长度会让不同 head 或不同块的 attention 计算量差异很大，若仍按常规方式分配给 GPU SM，会出现 straggler，拖低 kernel 利用率。Tangram 利用预算分布是静态已知这一点，离线预计算 workload 切分方案，把负载均衡从 runtime planner 挪到 ahead-of-time 阶段。这样 kernel 执行时不需要再做复杂调度，能更稳定地维持 SM 利用率。

从方法性质看，这不是单点优化，而是一个围绕“静态化异构结构”的系统级重构：先把 head-wise retention 视为模型固有属性，再据此重写内存分配、页组织和 kernel 调度。它和单纯改 attention kernel 或单纯改压缩策略不同，重点在于把算法侧的异构性转成系统侧可利用的确定性结构。7f:T8ca,The entire design is built on one observation: the retention budget needed by each attention head is relatively stable for a given model. Tangram uses that stability to turn an online heterogeneous-memory problem into a mostly static planning problem.

The first component is Deterministic Budget Allocation. A naive non-uniform KV system would reclaim memory dynamically as requests evolve, but that creates substantial control-plane overhead because the runtime must track and recover scattered pages for many heads. Tangram instead assigns deterministic per-head budgets ahead of time, converting dynamic reclamation into a preplanned memory footprint. The gain is lower runtime bookkeeping and simpler scheduling. The trade-off is reduced flexibility, but the paper argues that the head-wise pattern is stable enough that this is acceptable.

The second component is Head Group Page. Existing paged-KV designs use a monolithic page structure that works well when all heads have the same cache length. Under heterogeneous retention, that design causes severe internal fragmentation because compressed heads cannot reclaim memory cleanly at the right granularity. Tangram groups heads with similar budgets and gives each group its own page table. This makes physical memory reclamation better aligned with actual retention lengths. To keep page-table operations from becoming a CPU bottleneck, the system also introduces a vectorized block table implemented with CPU SIMD parallelism.

The third component is Ahead-of-Time Load Balancing. Non-uniform KV lengths create large differences in attention workload across heads and blocks. If the runtime uses standard scheduling, some GPU SMs become stragglers while others idle. Since the cache shape is known in advance from the deterministic budgets, Tangram moves load balancing offline and precomputes a workload distribution plan. This avoids runtime planning latency and improves kernel utilization under heterogeneous cache layouts.

What matters here is the overall design philosophy. Tangram does not optimize a single kernel in isolation. It treats head-wise heterogeneity as a predictable structural property and then co-designs memory management, paging, and execution around that property.80:T68f,The headline result is up to 2.6x end-to-end throughput improvement in multi-turn serving. That number matters because it is presented as a system-level outcome rather than a narrow kernel microbenchmark.

The evaluation is organized around the three bottlenecks identified earlier:
1. Memory efficiency: the paper compares how much GPU memory can actually be reclaimed under non-uniform compression, with a focus on the gap between theoretical compression and realized savings once fragmentation is accounted for.
2. Runtime overhead: it contrasts dynamic reclamation against deterministic budget allocation, showing that online management of scattered pages can become a major control-plane cost.
3. GPU utilization: it studies SM imbalance under heterogeneous KV lengths and measures how much Ahead-of-Time load balancing reduces stragglers and improves sustained throughput.

The experiments are centered on multi-turn dialogue serving, where KV cache growth is linear in the number of turns. The important question is not just whether compression reduces cache size on paper, but whether the system can maintain throughput as the conversation grows. Tangram is evaluated in the context of modern serving stacks rather than as a disconnected prototype, which makes the results more relevant.

From a research perspective, the most useful aspect of the experimental section is the separation between algorithmic savings and systems realization. The paper is effectively asking: once a compression method says it saved tokens, how much of that saving survives contact with memory layout, scheduling, and kernels? That framing is stronger than reporting compression ratio alone.81:T53c,This is a skim paper. The main value is in how clearly it decomposes the systems bottlenecks, not in mathematical detail. Starting from successful trajectories, the authors intervene on a given HTML observation by removing pieces of information and asking which minimal subset causes the task to fail when removed. This is more informative than node-level ablation because it separates the role of text content, tag identity, and attribute values.

Once an MFS is constructed for each step, the paper defines coverage: whether a reduction method fully retains the MFS for that instance, aggregated over the dataset. Coverage is proposed as a proxy for end-to-end success rate. The practical advantage is large: after MFS construction, evaluation requires neither web access nor policy-model inference, and instances can be scored independently in parallel.

Using this framework, the authors compare 11 classes of reduction methods, including heuristic pruning, retrieval-based selection, LLM-guided selection, and accessibility-tree variants. They then use coverage as an optimization objective and apply GEPA, an LLM-based evolutionary optimization framework, to learn benchmark-specific pruning programs. The resulting message is fairly clear: generic LLM-based reducers can preserve more critical information, but their own latency is often too high; benchmark-specific program optimization is a better route if the goal is lower total step latency.84:T634,The experiments are centered on validating coverage as a proxy and quantifying the real trade-off between preservation quality and latency.

1. The motivation is backed by a concrete cost number: on WorkArena L1, evaluating 11 methods across 32 configurations and 33 tasks with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B took 232.4 cumulative hours. That makes exhaustive end-to-end comparison impractical.

2. On both WorkArena L1 and WebLinx, coverage is shown to correlate strongly with end-to-end success rate, while enabling more than 100x speedup in cumulative evaluation time. If this correlation is robust, it makes offline screening of reduction methods much more feasible.

3. In the method comparison, LLM inference-based reducers achieve higher coverage than retrieval-based methods, especially under aggressive reduction, but they incur substantially higher latency. So better reduction quality does not necessarily translate into lower system latency.

4. The paper also finds benchmark-specific differences in what information matters: text content is more critical on WebLinx, whereas HTML tags and attributes matter more on WorkArena L1. This explains why a single generic reduction policy may not transfer well.

First, FBHM. The dataset is built along two orthogonal axes. The functionality axis contains 25 curated multimodal hate mechanisms grouped into five broader families: visual format and imagery type, textual obfuscation and lexical evasion, structural composition and visual metaphor, pragmatic inference and sentiment mismatch, and non-hateful/counterspeech contrasts. This enables near-causal comparisons: same mechanism across targets, or same target across mechanisms. The final dataset has 5,000 memes from 500 base items, with 500 examples reserved as a steering set and 4,500 as test data. Annotation is expert-driven, and the reported Cohen’s kappa of 0.84 on independently reviewed base items suggests solid label consistency.

Second, LSV, or learnable steering vectors. Instead of updating model weights, the method learns a set of layer-wise continuous intervention vectors for a frozen VLM. Each transformer layer receives a steering vector matching the hidden dimension, together with a learned scalar coefficient controlling intervention strength at that layer. The optimization objective is framed as a causal-style intervention on internal representations using the small steering set. The key design choice is to move the model in activation space rather than parameter space. Compared with PEFT/LoRA, this reduces the risk of overwriting the original task behavior; compared with in-context learning, it provides a persistent, layer-aware modification rather than a prompt-local effect. The learned per-layer scaling is important because the method does not assume all layers should be perturbed equally.8b:T4de,The main empirical result is a severe generalization collapse. For a pretraining-oriented reader, 20–30 minutes is enough to extract the main lessons. The most transferable parts are the controlled evaluation design and the activation-space repair strategy.8d:T762,TraceGraph has a clear pipeline.

First, each action–observation step in a rollout is encoded into a sparse observable signature. Model identity is intentionally excluded at this stage so that the graph is built from shared external behavior rather than from model-specific metadata. Similarity between states is computed using IDF-weighted Jaccard, which gives more weight to rarer, more informative observable features. Using pooled trajectories from multiple models, the method constructs a mutual-kNN graph over these states.

Second, the graph is structurally decomposed using tools such as biconnected components and articulation gates. This gives a task-specific topology with stable regions and bottlenecks. Only after the graph is built does the method overlay outcome information. Successful trajectories define productive cores; failure-associated recurring regions define traps. This separation is important: the graph is meant to be a shared descriptive map first, not a supervised predictor from the start.

Third, each rollout is summarized by three events: Access, whether it reaches a productive core; Trap exposure, whether it enters a trap region; and Repair, whether it returns from a trap to a core. This is a deliberately compact process profile. Instead of reconstructing all reasoning details, the paper keeps the smallest set of events that can explain benchmark-specific process demands.

The paper then uses the same trap overlay for online intervention. On SWE-bench, when a live trajectory enters a historically risky region, the system triggers a prefix-fork recovery pipeline. Continuations resume from the same state with lightweight modifications such as a conservative diagnosis note or a temperature bump. The point is not that the recovery policy is sophisticated; the point is that graph-derived traps are actionable enough to support runtime control.8e:T505,The evaluation spans five benchmark splits, 7,329 trajectories, 427 tasks, and five models. The main result is qualitative but operationally meaningful: models with similar aggregate scores can exhibit very different navigation styles on the shared graph. Some explore broadly and rely on repair, some avoid traps early but access productive cores less often, and some reach productive regions frequently while also exposing themselves to more traps. This shows that benchmark scores alone do not reveal what process a benchmark rewards.

The intervention experiment focuses on SWE-bench because it shows the clearest positive demand for Repair. Using the TraceGraph-derived trap detector as a runtime trigger, the trap-aware prefix-fork pipeline is tested on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances. The best pooled policy improves resolved rate by +3.1 points on the per-provider fired subset (p=0.016) and by +3.8 points on common-fired instances (p=0.045). The gains are modest, but they matter because they demonstrate that the trap regions are not merely post-hoc explanations; they can support online recovery. The paper also notes that the effective recovery component differs by provider, suggesting provider-specific failure modes rather than a single universal repair strategy.8f:T463,Read it as an evaluation-method paper, not as a new agent architecture paper.
1. Start with Figures 1 and 2. They explain the shared decision landscape idea, the graph construction pipeline, and the three rollout events.
2. Then read the state encoding and graph-building details: observable keys, IDF-weighted Jaccard, mutual-kNN, and the BCC / articulation-gate decomposition. These choices determine whether trajectories from different models are aligned in a meaningful way.
3. Next, inspect the benchmark-level process profiles. The useful question is not which model ranks first, but which benchmarks reward trap avoidance versus trap recovery.

The design choices that matter:
- Prompt construction is grounded in observed Chinese online evasion practices rather than web scraping or model-generated adversarial prompts, aiming to reduce leakage into pretraining corpora and avoid the “model generates attacks in its own distribution” problem.
- A nine-category obfuscation taxonomy is introduced to slice failures by evasion mechanism (e.g., Pinyin substitution vs. radical decomposition vs. slang), which is particularly diagnostic for tokenizer/script robustness.
- Labels target deployment-relevant response strategies: REFUSE, SAFE-REDIRECT, RESPOND, enabling evaluation of both under-blocking and over-blocking. The paper explicitly positions model benchmarking as future work; the present focus is on producing a stable, carefully annotated benchmark and taxonomy.91:T7c6,The method has two parts. First, the paper formalizes behavioral indistinguishability as an empirical, bounded claim rather than an absolute property. A student S is (epsilon, q, t, A)-behaviorally indistinguishable from teacher T if no adversary in class A, with query budget q and compute budget t, can distinguish their outputs with advantage greater than epsilon over a specified prompt distribution. This framing matters because it forces the evaluation to state what prompts are considered, what attacker is allowed, and what resources are available.

Second, the authors instantiate this definition with a multi-view evaluation pipeline instead of a single metric. They use: (1) response-only discriminators to detect stylistic or surface artifacts; (2) prompt-response discriminators to test whether the answer is teacher-like in context; (3) semantic similarity metrics; (4) policy-level agreement measures for safety and refusal behavior; and (5) a pairwise teacher-identification judge that sees two answers to the same prompt and decides which one is more likely from the teacher. They also apply A/B-swap consistency filtering to reduce judge position bias.

The empirical setup uses two model families, Qwen and Llama. For each family, they compare the teacher, the original base student, and a LoRA-distilled student trained on black-box teacher responses. The choice of LoRA is important: it reflects a realistic low-cost distillation regime and also means the paper is measuring how much behavior can be transferred through limited-capacity adaptation, not through full-parameter imitation.

A further practical component is data acquisition under query budget. The paper compares disagreement-guided sampling against stratified random sampling. The result is notable: disagreement-guided acquisition does not consistently outperform the simpler coverage-oriented baseline, suggesting that diversity and category coverage remain strong defaults for behavioral distillation.92:T71c,The experiments are built around a controlled 5,000-prompt behavioral probe suite covering general QA, reasoning, coding, summarization, style/format control, ambiguous prompts, safety-boundary prompts, instruction conflict, domain-technical questions, and robustness perturbations. The authors explicitly position this as a probe distribution rather than a natural deployment distribution.

Three findings stand out. First, LoRA distillation improves semantic similarity and makes learned discriminators less effective, so black-box response distillation does transfer a substantial portion of observable behavior. Second, this does not imply behavioral indistinguishability. The clearest number comes from the pairwise teacher-identification setup: for the Qwen family, distinguishing advantage drops from 0.158 for the base student to 0.081 after LoRA distillation. That is a meaningful reduction, but still clearly above zero. Third, residual distinguishability is concentrated in specific categories rather than spread uniformly. Style/format prompts, robustness perturbations, and domain-technical prompts remain the easiest places to tell teacher and student apart. This suggests that distillation learns answer content more readily than stable response policy and boundary behavior.

The query-budget experiments also matter. Under limited API calls, disagreement-guided acquisition does not consistently beat stratified random sampling. That is a useful practical result: if the goal is behavioral transfer, broad prompt coverage may be more reliable than more elaborate active-selection heuristics.

Overall, the evidence is cumulative rather than tied to one metric. Semantic similarity improves, discriminators weaken, and pairwise judging becomes harder, but none of these indicate full behavioral matching.93:T48e,Start with the introduction, especially the distinction between output matching and behavioral indistinguishability. That is the central framing move. Then read the formalization section carefully to understand what epsilon, q, t, A, and the prompt distribution are doing in the definition. After that, focus on the evaluation design and the main pipeline figure, because the novelty is in how the paper operationalizes indistinguishability rather than in a new training method.

If reading selectively, prioritize three parts: (1) the pairwise teacher-identification protocol and A/B-swap consistency filtering; (2) the construction of the 5,000-prompt probe suite; and (3) the category-wise results plus the query-budget comparison. These sections tell you whether the framework is credible and whether it changes practical distillation choices.

A useful skim should take about 25 to 35 minutes. If your work touches API distillation or extraction defense, it is worth checking the appendix for discriminator training details, judge prompts, and acquisition settings, since those implementation choices can materially affect the measured distinguishing advantage.94:T7bb,The work has two main components. The first is the Social AI Design Code. Instead of jumping directly to benchmark construction, the authors define a normative framework for social interaction. The code centers on three principles: models should not encourage users to treat AI as human, should not increase emotional attachment in ways that undermine welfare, and should not push users toward extended engagement when doing so is harmful. Each principle is translated into concrete design requirements that can be checked in model responses. This is an important design choice: the benchmark is not evaluating extreme opt-in role-play settings, but the default behavior of conversational systems.

The second component is the EUDAIMONIA benchmark itself. The data source is WildChat rather than fully synthetic prompts. The authors run a multi-stage curation pipeline over 3.2 million real user prompts: weak-to-strong filtration to surface candidate risky interactions, multi-model relabeling to identify which design requirements each input can trigger, and controlled rewriting of near-miss examples to improve coverage while preserving topic and tone. The final benchmark contains 969 unique user inputs and 3,147 violation checks. The key unit is not just the prompt, but the prompt-requirement pair, which allows more granular analysis of where models fail.

The benchmark design is trying to avoid two common weaknesses. One is reducing social risk to isolated capabilities such as sycophancy or anthropomorphism without tying them to user welfare. The other is relying too heavily on synthetic prompts that miss the texture of real user interactions. Using real-world prompts and then augmenting them through controlled rewriting is a sensible compromise between ecological validity and coverage. Another notable design choice is the explicit test of whether extended thinking reduces violations, which helps separate reasoning deficits from deeper alignment tendencies.95:T5a0,Three findings stand out clearly from the provided text. First, even strong frontier models still fail often on this benchmark. The paper reports violation rates of 30.7% for Claude-Opus-4.7 and 27.2% for GPT-5.5 as of April 2026. That is a meaningful failure rate given that these are among the strongest available models. Second, the most common failure modes include implying that AI can replace human relationships and failing to clearly disclose that the system is an AI. These map directly onto dependence risk and anthropomorphism risk. Third, extended thinking does not reduce violation rates, which supports the authors' claim that these are persistent social-alignment failures rather than problems that disappear with more test-time reasoning.

The paper also appears to compare multiple model families and generations. The text notes that while some closed-source families improve over time, several regress on intentionally human-like speech. That matters because it suggests these harms are not one-off bugs that stay fixed once patched; they can reappear as product tone, personality shaping, or helpfulness optimization changes.
